title: Sequences, recurrences and limits
summary: Sequences defined by a rule: bound them, find their limit, prove periodicity or eventual behaviour. Linear recurrences solve by characteristic roots; non-linear ones by monotonicity and invariants.
key_statements: a_{n+2} = pa_{n+1} + qa_n \Rightarrow a_n = \alpha r_1^n + \beta r_2^n
why: Discrete dynamical systems start here; the Collatz problem shows how quickly simple rules become intractable.

title: Floor functions and fractional parts
summary: Identities and estimates for $\lfloor x\rfloor$ and $\{x\} = x - \lfloor x\rfloor$, Beatty sequences, and equidistribution of $\{n\alpha\}$.
why: Counting lattice points under a curve is a floor sum; Weyl's equidistribution theorem is about fractional parts.

title: Linear algebra methods in combinatorics
summary: Vector spaces, rank and determinants as tools: bound a family by showing its members are linearly independent in a space of known dimension.
why: The dimension argument gives some of the sharpest bounds in combinatorics (Frankl–Wilson, Fisher's inequality).

title: Angles, triangles and similarity
summary: Angle chasing, congruent and similar triangles, the laws of sines and cosines, and areas. Nearly every olympiad geometry solution is built from these.
why: Euclid's Elements is the first axiomatic theory; its parallel postulate led to non-Euclidean geometry.
references: Chen, Euclidean Geometry in Mathematical Olympiads

leads_to.title: Vectors in the plane and in space
Circles and power of a point

timeline.title: Euclid's Elements
timeline.text: Axiomatic plane geometry; Book IX also proves there are infinitely many primes.

title: Circles and power of a point
summary: Inscribed angles, cyclic quadrilaterals, tangents, and the power of a point $P$ with respect to a circle: for any line through $P$ meeting the circle at $A,B$, $PA\cdot PB$ is constant.
why: Radical axes and coaxal circles organise most configurations with several circles.
references: Chen, Euclidean Geometry in Mathematical Olympiads

title: Triangle centres and classical configurations
summary: Incentre, circumcentre, orthocentre, centroid and their circles: the Euler line, the nine-point circle, the incircle and excircles, Ceva's and Menelaus's theorems.
why: Recognising a standard configuration is often the whole solution.
references: Chen, Euclidean Geometry in Mathematical Olympiads

prerequisites.title: Circles and power of a point

title: Transformations and inversion
summary: Homotheties, rotations, reflections, spiral similarities and inversion map a configuration to a simpler one. Inversion turns circles through the centre into lines.
key_statements: P \mapsto P' \text{ on ray } OP,\ \ OP\cdot OP' = r^2
why: Thinking in transformations is Klein's Erlangen programme: a geometry is the study of invariants of a group.
references: Chen, Euclidean Geometry in Mathematical Olympiads
